text: A police‑officer may arrest a person without a warrant when the person commits a cognizable offence in the officer’s presence, or when there is a reasonable complaint, credible information or reasonable suspicion that the person has committed a cognizable offence (whether punishable up to seven years or more) and the officer believes the arrest is necessary to prevent further offence, to investigate, to preserve evidence or to stop intimidation. The provision also lists other specific situations such as a person in possession of a house‑breaking implement, a proclaimed offender, someone found with suspected stolen property, anyone who obstructs a police‑officer, a deserter from the armed forces, a person involved in an act abroad that would be an offence in Bangladesh, a released convict breaching a rule, or when a requisition for arrest has been received from another officer. The officer may not arrest for the purpose of preventive detention.

citations.quote: Any police-officer may, without an order from a Magistrate and without warrant, arrest- firstly, any person who commits, in the presence of a police-officer, a cognizable offence; secondly, any person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence ... if the following conditions are satisfied, namely:- (i) the police-officer has reason to believe ... and (ii) the police-officer is satisfied that such arrest is necessary- (a) to prevent such person from committing any further offence; or (b) for proper investigation of the offence; or (c) to prevent such person from causing the evidence of the offence to disappear ...

thirdly, any person against whom credible information has been received that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to more than seven years whether with or without fine, or with death sentence ...

fourthly, any person having in his possession without lawful excuse, the burden of proving which excuse shall lie on such person, any implement of house breaking; fifthly, any person who has been proclaimed as an offender ... sixthly, any person in whose possession anything is found which may reasonably be suspected to be stolen property ...

seventhly, any person who obstructs a police-officer while in the execution of his duty ... eighthly, any person ... deserter from the armed forces of Bangladesh; ninthly, any person ... act ... out of Bangladesh, which, if committed in Bangladesh, would have been punishable as an offence ...

eleventhly, any person for whose arrest a requisition, has been received from another police-officer, provided that the requisition specifies the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made ...
(2) No police-officer shall arrest a person under this section for the purpose of detaining him under any law providing for preventive detention.

text: Police may detain a person arrested without a warrant for up to twenty‑four hours (excluding travel time to the Magistrate’s Court) unless a special order under section 167 is obtained. They must otherwise bring the arrested person before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay.

citations.quote: shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 167, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.

shall, without unnecessary delay and subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail, take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police-station.

text: The search of a woman must be carried out by another woman, observing strict decency.

citations.quote: Whenever it is necessary to cause a woman to be searched, the search shall be made by another woman, with strict regard to decency.

text: Only the amount of restraint that is necessary to prevent the arrested person’s escape may be used; no more restraint than that is permitted.

citations.quote: The person arrested shall not be subjected to more restraint than is necessary to prevent his escape.

In making an arrest the police-officer or other person making the same shall actually touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested, unless there be a submission to the custody by word or action.

text:
When making an arrest a police officer must: 
1. Bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name. 
2. Disclose his identity and, if demanded, show his identity card to the arrested person and any witnesses. 
3. Prepare a memorandum of arrest that is attested by a suitable witness and have the arrested person countersign it. 
4. Inform a family member, relative or nominated friend of the arrest within 24 hours, giving the time, place of arrest and place of custody. 
5. If the arrested person has any injury, ensure medical examination and first‑aid, obtain a medical certificate and record the reasons for the injury. 
6. Allow the arrested person, if he wishes, to consult a lawyer of his choice or meet a close relative, preferably within twelve hours of the arrest.

citations.quote: (a) bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name which will facilitate easy identification;
(b) disclose his identity and if demanded, shall show his identity card to the person arrested and to the persons present at the time of arrest;

(c) prepare a memorandum of arrest which shall be- (i)attested by at least one witness, who is a member of the family of the person arrested or a respectable inhabitant of the locality where the arrest is made and where no such witness is available, the reasons thereof be recorded in the memorandum;
(ii) countersigned or thumb-impressed by the person arrested if not refused by him;

(d) intimate, where the accused is arrested from a place other than his residence, to a family member, relative, or a friend nominated by the person arrested, as soon as practicable but not later than twenty four hours from the time of such arrest, notifying the time and place of arrest and the place of custody;

(e) ensure, if any mark of injury is found on the body of the person arrested, the examination and first aid treatment of the person by a medical officer or a registered medical practitioner, as the case may be, in accordance with section 46E; obtain a certificate from the attending medical officer or practitioner; and record the reasons for such injury;
(f) allow the person arrested, if he so desires, to consult a lawyer of his choice or to meet any of his nearest relation, preferably within twelve hours of such arrest.

text: Yes. The Code of Criminal Procedure requires that a police officer inform the person being arrested of the reasons for the arrest at the time of the arrest.

citations.quote: Every police-officer arresting any person without warrant shall, at the time of making arrest, communicate to him the reasons for which he is arrested.
the police-officer shall record while making such arrest, his reasons in writing

text: When information about a cognizable offence is given to the officer in charge of a police‑station, it must be reduced to writing (or written directly), read back to the informant, signed by the informant, and entered in a book kept by that officer in the form prescribed by the Government.

citations.quote: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence if given orally to an officer in charge of a police‑station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the Government may prescribe in this behalf.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, a police officer may not investigate a non‑cognizable offence unless a Magistrate orders the investigation.

citations.quote: No police-officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate of the first or second class having power to try such case

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure an officer in charge of a police‑station may investigate a cognizable case without a Magistrate’s order.

citations.quote: Any officer in charge of a police-station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case

text: Yes. Under section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a police officer conducting an investigation may, by a written order, require the attendance of any person who appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case, and that person must attend as required.

citations.quote: may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself of any person ... who, from the information given or otherwise, appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case; and such person shall attend as so required.

text: No. A person examined by a police officer is bound to answer all questions except those whose answers would tend to expose him to a criminal charge, penalty, or forfeiture.

citations.quote: Such person shall be bound to answer all questions relating to such case put to him by such officer, other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture.

text: No. Under section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a statement made to a police officer, if reduced to writing, must not be signed by the person who made it.

citations.quote: No statement made by any person to a police-officer in the course of an investigation ... shall, if reduced into writing, be signed by the person making it

text: No. A police officer is prohibited from offering any inducement, threat or promise to obtain a statement.

citations.quote: No police-officer or other person in authority shall offer or make, or cause to be offered or made, any such inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in the Evidence Act, 1872, section 24.

text: A Magistrate who is a Metropolitan Magistrate, a Magistrate of the first class, or a Magistrate of the second class specially empowered by the Government (and who is not a police‑officer) may record a confession. Before doing so, the Magistrate must tell the person that he is not obliged to confess and that any confession he makes may be used as evidence against him.

citations.quote: Any Metropolitan Magistrate, any Magistrate of the first class and any Magistrate of the second class specially empowered in this behalf by the Government may, if he is not a police‑officer record any statement or confession...
A Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so it may be used as evidence against him...

text: If an investigation cannot be finished within the 24‑hour period, the police officer must immediately send a copy of the diary entries to the nearest Judicial Magistrate and forward the accused to that magistrate. The magistrate may then order a medical examination of the accused before he is handed over to police custody, and if any injury or claim of torture is shown, the magistrate must direct another medical examination. The magistrate can also authorize detention of the accused in police custody for up to fifteen days, or, if he lacks jurisdiction to try the case, order the accused to be sent to a magistrate who does have jurisdiction.

citations.quote: shall forthwith transmit to the [nearest Judicial Magistrate] a copy of the entries in the diary hereinafter prescribed relating to the case, and shall at the same time forward the accused to such Magistrate.

may order that the accused be examined by a medical officer of nearest government hospital before he is handed over to such custody; and upon expiry of the period of police custody, the accused shall be produced before the Magistrate without unnecessary delay; and if, upon such production, there appears to be any mark of injury on the body of the person accused, or the accused alleges that he has been subjected to torture during such custody, the Magistrate shall direct that the accused be examined by a medical officer of the nearest government hospital

may, whether he has or has not jurisdiction to try the case from time to time authorize the detention of the accused in such custody as such Magistrate thinks fit, for a term not exceeding fifteen days in the whole; and if he has not jurisdiction to try the case or send it for trial, and considers further detention unnecessary, he may order the accused to be forwarded to a Magistrate having such jurisdiction

text: A Magistrate may take cognizance of an offence (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute the offence; (b) upon a written report of such facts made by a police‑officer; or (c) upon information from any person other than a police‑officer, or on his own knowledge or suspicion that the offence has been committed.

citations.quote: may take cognizance of any offence- (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence; (b) upon a report in writing of such facts made by any police-officer; (c) upon information received from any person other than a police-officer, or upon his own knowledge or suspicion, that such offence has been committed.

text: When a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on a complaint, he must immediately examine the complainant (and any witnesses present, if he considers it necessary) on oath, reduce the substance of that examination to writing, and have it signed by the complainant or witness and by the Magistrate. However, if the complaint is made in writing, the examination is not required, and likewise when the written complaint is made by a Court or a public servant acting in official duties.

citations.quote: A Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence on complaint shall at once examine ... and the substance of the examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed ...
when the complaint is made in writing, nothing herein contained shall be deemed to require [such examination] ...

text: A Magistrate may postpone issuing process against the person complained about when, on receiving a complaint of an offence that he is authorised to take cognizance of (or that has been transferred to him under section 192), he thinks it appropriate and records his reasons in writing. This postponement is allowed to enable an inquiry or investigation to ascertain the truth or falsehood of the complaint, provided that, unless the complaint was made by a Court, the requirements of section 200 have been complied with, and even where the offence is triable exclusively by a Court of Session the Magistrate may still postpone the issue of process.

citations.quote: Any Magistrate, on receipt of a complaint of an offence ... may, if he thinks fit, for reasons to be recorded in writing, postpone the issue of process for compelling the attendance of the person complained against ...
Provided that, save where the complaint has been made by a Court, no such direction shall be made unless the provisions of section 200 have been complied with.

text: A magistrate may dismiss a complaint when, after considering the complainant’s statement on oath (if any) and the result of any investigation or inquiry, he judges that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding.

citations.quote: there is in his judgment no sufficient ground for proceeding

text: An accused must be discharged before a charge is framed when (i) the Magistrate, after considering the record and hearing both sides, finds the charge to be groundless (section 241A); (ii) the Public Prosecutor withdraws the prosecution before a charge has been framed (section 494(a)); or (iii) after an inquiry under section 117 it is shown that no bond is required, the Magistrate discharges the person (section 119).

citations.quote: if the Magistrate ... considers the charge to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing.
if it is made before a charge has been framed, the accused shall be discharged in respect of such offence or offences
shall ... discharge him.

text: If the complainant does not appear on the day fixed for the accused’s appearance (or any later adjourned date), the magistrate must acquit the accused, unless the magistrate decides it is appropriate to adjourn the hearing to another day.

citations.quote: the Magistrate shall, notwithstanding anything herein before contained, acquit the accused, unless for some reason he thinks proper to adjoin the hearing of the case to some other day

text: When a magistrate is satisfied that an accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious, he must record the reasons and may direct the complainant or informant to pay compensation to the accused (up to the prescribed maximum), may call the complainant to show cause why he should not pay, and if the complainant does not appear may issue a summons. The magistrate may also, in the same order, impose a default imprisonment of up to thirty days, and may further order imprisonment of up to six months or a fine of up to one lakh taka.

citations.quote: if he is satisfied that the accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious ... direct that compensation ... not exceeding [fifty thousand Taka] ... be paid by such complainant or informant to the accused

The Magistrate may, by the order directing payment of the compensation under sub-section (2), further order that, in default of payment, the person ordered to pay such compensation shall suffer simple imprisonment for a period not exceeding thirty days.

the Magistrate may, in addition to the order directing payment of the compensation under sub-section (2), further order that the person ordered to pay such compensation shall also suffer imprisonment for a period not exceeding six months or pay a fine not exceeding [one lac taka].

call upon him forthwith to show cause why he should not pay compensation to such accused ... or, if such person is not present direct the issue of a summons to him to appear and show cause as aforesaid.

text: A Metropolitan Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class may tender a pardon to an accomplice. This power can be used in the case of (i) any offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session, (ii) any offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, (iii) any offence punishable under section 211 of the Penal Code with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, or (iv) any offence under sections 216A, 369, 401, 435 or 477A of the Penal Code.

citations.quote: In the case of any offence triable exclusively by the ... Court of Session, or any offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, or any offence punishable under section 211 of the Penal Code, with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, or any offence under any of the following sections of the Penal Code, namely, sections 216A, 369, 401, 435 and 477A, [a Metropolitan Magistrate] or any Magistrate of the first class may ... tender a pardon to such person

text: An accused may be tried in his absence when the court is satisfied that he has absconded or is concealing himself and there is no immediate prospect of arrest, after the court has ordered him to appear and he fails to do so; also when, after having been produced or released on bail, the accused again absconds or fails to appear, the court may record its decision and try him in absentia; and when the judge or magistrate is satisfied, for recorded reasons, that the accused is incapable of remaining before the court and the accused is represented by an advocate, the court may dispense with his attendance and proceed with the trial in his absence. In cases where an accused has absconded and cannot be arrested, the court may also examine witnesses and record their depositions in his absence for use as evidence.

citations.quote: where the Court has reason to believe that an accused person has absconded or is concealing himself so that he cannot be arrested and produced for trial and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him ... if such person fails to comply with such direction, he shall be tried in his absence

Where in a case after the production or appearance of an accused before the Court or his release on bail, the accused person absconds or fails to appear ... the Court ... shall, recording its decision so to do, try such person in his absence

if the Judge or Magistrate is satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, that any one or more of [the] accused is or are incapable of remaining before the Court, he may, if such accused is represented by [an advocate], dispense with his attendance and proceed with such inquiry or trial in his absence

If it is proved that an accused person has absconded, and that there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, the Court ... may, in his absence, examine the witnesses ... and record their depositions

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a person who refuses to answer questions put to him by a criminal court may be punished. Section 485 allows the court to sentence such a person to simple imprisonment or to commit him to custody for up to seven days if he offers no reasonable excuse.

citations.quote: If any witness or person ... refuses to answer such questions ... the Court may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, sentence him to simple imprisonment, or ... commit him to the custody of an officer of the Court for any term not exceeding seven days

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a criminal court is deemed an open court and the public generally may have access, subject to the judge’s power to restrict access when he thinks fit.

citations.quote: The place in which any Criminal Court is held ... shall be deemed an open Court, to which the public generally may have access, so far as the same can conveniently contain them: Provided that the presiding Judge or Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, order ... that the public generally, or any particular person, shall not have access
The word “public” includes any class of the public or any community.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a person who has been acquitted cannot be tried again for the same offence while that acquittal remains in force.

citations.quote: A person who has once been tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction for an offence and ... acquitted of such offence shall, while such conviction or acquittal remains in force, not be liable to be tried again for the same offence

text: An appeal against an order of acquittal may be presented either by the Government (by directing the Public Prosecutor to file the appeal) or by the complainant themselves, subject to the conditions in the statute.

citations.quote: the Government may, in any case, direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal- (a) to the High Court Division from an original or appellate Order of acquittal passed by any Court of Session; (b) to the Court of Session from an original or appellate Order of acquittal passed by any Magistrate.

the complainant may present an appeal- (a) to the High Court Division from an original order of acquittal passed by any Court of Session; (b) to the Court of Session from an original order of acquittal passed by any Magistrate.

text: The High Court Division may, whenever it thinks fit, issue directions to (a) bring a person within its appellate criminal jurisdiction before the Court for legal disposition; (b) set at liberty a person who is illegally or improperly detained in public or private custody; (c) bring a prisoner detained in a jail within its limits before the Court to be examined as a witness; (d) bring a prisoner before a Court‑martial or any Commissioners for trial or examination of matters pending before them; and (e) remove a prisoner from one custody to another for the purpose of trial.

citations.quote: that a person within the limits of its appellate criminal jurisdiction be brought up before the Court to be dealt with according to law; (b) that a person illegally or improperly detained in public or private custody with such limits be set at liberty; (c) that a prisoner detained in any jail situate within such limits be brought before the Court to be there examined as a witness; (d) that a prisoner detained as aforesaid be brought before a Court‑martial or any Commissioners for trial or to be examined touching any matter pending before such Court‑martial or Commissioners respectively; (e) that a prisoner within such limits be removed from one custody to another for the purpose of trial

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, a person who is not accused of a non‑bailable offence (i.e., accused of a bailable offence) and who is prepared to give bail must be released on bail, although the officer or court may instead accept a bond without sureties.

citations.quote: When any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence ... is prepared at any time while in the custody of such officer or at any stage of the proceedings before such Court to give bail, such person shall be released on bail

text: Bail may be granted to a person accused of a non‑bailable offence when he is arrested or detained without warrant, or when he appears before a Court, provided that there are no reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life. The Court may also order bail for a person under sixteen years of age, any woman, or any sick or infirm accused of such an offence. Additionally, if the officer or Court finds that there are no reasonable grounds to believe the accused has committed a non‑bailable offence but there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry, the accused may be released on bail pending that inquiry.

citations.quote: When any person accused of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police-station, or appears or is brought before a Court, he may be released on bail, but he shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life: Provided that the Court may direct that any person under the age of sixteen years or any woman or any sick or infirm person accused of such offence be released on bail.

If it appears to such officer or Court at any stage of the investigation, inquiry or trial, as the case may be, that there are not reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed a non-bailable offence, but that there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry into his guilt, the accused shall, pending such inquiry, be released on bail...

text: Yes, the amount of a bail bond can be reduced, and this can be ordered by the High Court Division or a Court of Session.

citations.quote: the High Court Division or Court of Session may, in any case, whether there be an appeal on conviction or not, direct that any person be admitted to bail, or that the bail required by a police-officer or Magistrate be reduced.

text: When a trial is concluded, the court may order the disposal of any property or document produced before it or in its custody that is connected with the offence, by destruction, confiscation, delivery to a person claiming entitlement, or any other manner it deems fit.

citations.quote: When an inquiry or a trial in any Criminal Court is concluded, the Court may make such order as it thinks fit for the disposal by destruction, confiscation, or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession thereof or otherwise of any property or document produced before it or in its custody or regarding which any offence appears to have been committed, or which has been used for the commission of any offence.

text: The High Court Division retains its inherent power to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under the Code, to prevent abuse of the process of any Court, and otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

citations.quote: Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent power of the High Court Division to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

text: A District Magistrate, or any other Executive Magistrate who has been specially empowered by the Government or the District Magistrate to act under section 144, may issue such an order in an urgent case.

citations.quote: In cases where, in the opinion of a District Magistrate, [or any other Executive Magistrate] specially empowered by the Government or the District Magistrate to act under this section, ... such Magistrate may, by a written order ... direct any person to abstain from a certain act

text: When a magistrate is satisfied, on the basis of a police report or other information, that a dispute over land or water is likely to cause a breach of the peace, he must issue a written order calling the parties to appear before his court and to give written statements of their claims. The magistrate then examines those statements, hears the parties, takes any evidence he thinks necessary and, if possible, decides which party was in possession at the date of the order (treating a party who was forcibly dispossessed within two months as if in possession). If he decides a party is entitled to possession, he issues an order declaring that party’s right to possession until lawfully evicted. The magistrate may also attach the disputed property pending his decision.

citations.quote: Whenever ... is satisfied ... that a dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace exists ... he shall make an order in writing, ... requiring the parties concerned ... to attend his Court ... and to put in written statements of their respective claims

The Magistrate shall then, without reference to the merits ... peruse the statements ... hear the parties, receive all such evidence ... and, if possible, decide whether any and which of the parties was ... in possession of the said subject
If the Magistrate decides that one of the parties ... be treated as being in such possession ... he shall issue an order declaring such party to be entitled to possession thereof

text: A magistrate may require a person to execute a bond for keeping the peace when, on information that the person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb public tranquillity, the magistrate is of the opinion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding, and may order the bond after the person is shown cause why it should not be required. The magistrate may also direct the execution of such a bond when he considers that immediate measures are necessary to prevent a breach of the peace, a disturbance of public tranquillity, or the commission of any offence.

citations.quote: Whenever [a District Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate] is informed that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity ... the Magistrate if in his opinion there is sufficient ground for proceeding may ... require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for keeping the peace

the Magistrate, if he considers that immediate measures are necessary for the prevention of a breach of the peace or disturbance of the public tranquillity or the commission of any offence ... may ... direct the person ... to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for keeping the peace

text: Yes. When a person is arrested without a warrant, the police officer must, without unnecessary delay, take or send the arrested person before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police‑station.

citations.quote: A police-officer making an arrest without warrant shall, without unnecessary delay and subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail, take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police-station.

text: The officer must give the subordinate a written order that specifies the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made.

citations.quote: he shall deliver to the officer required to make the arrest an order in writing, specifying the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made.

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, an officer who arrests a person may search that person and seize any articles found on him, except for necessary clothing.

citations.quote: may search such person, and place in safe custody all articles, other than necessary wearing-apparel, found upon him

text: A person may be detained for up to twenty‑four hours (excluding travel time) before a Magistrate must give a special order under section 167 for any further detention.

citations.quote: shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 167, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.

text: For a cognizable offence, any information given orally to the officer in charge of a police‑station must be reduced to writing, read back to the informant, signed by the informant and entered in the police‑station’s book. For a non‑cognizable offence, the officer only records the substance of the information in the book and refers the informant to a Magistrate; the police may not investigate the case unless a Magistrate orders it, and even then they may investigate only with the same powers as in a cognizable case, except they cannot arrest without a warrant.

citations.quote: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence if given orally to an officer in charge of a police-station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the Government may prescribe in this behalf.

When information is given to an officer in charge of a police-station of the commission within the limits of such station of a non-cognizable offence, he shall enter in a book to be kept as aforesaid the substance of such information and refer the informant to the Magistrate.
No police-officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate of the first or second class having power to try such case or [send] the same for trial.

Any police-officer receiving such order may exercise the same powers in respect of the investigation (except the power to arrest without warrant) as an officer in charge of a police-station may exercise in a cognizable case.

text: The police must tell the arrested person the reasons for his arrest at the time of arrest, and must put those reasons in writing as a record of the arrest.

citations.quote: communicate to him the reasons for which he is arrested.
record while making such arrest, his reasons in writing

text: For bailable offences (any offence that is not a non‑bailable offence), the law says that when the accused is prepared to give bail he "shall be released on bail" and the officer or court may instead discharge him on a bond without sureties. For non‑bailable offences, bail is not a right: the accused "may be released on bail, but he shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life". However, the court must still release a minor, a woman, or a sick or infirm person on bail, and if there are no reasonable grounds to believe the accused committed the non‑bailable offence, bail may be granted pending further inquiry. Thus, bailable offences guarantee bail on request, while non‑bailable offences allow bail only at the discretion of the officer or court and subject to serious‑offence safeguards.

citations.quote: When any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence ... is prepared ... to give bail, such person shall be released on bail: Provided that such officer or Court, if he or it thinks fit, may, instead of taking bail from such person, discharge him on his executing a bond without sureties

When any person accused of any non-bailable offence ... he may be released on bail, but he shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life: Provided that the Court may direct that any person under the age of sixteen years or any woman or any sick or infirm person accused of such an offence be released on bail

text: The extracts set out safeguards only for confessions recorded by a Magistrate. Before recording a confession, the Magistrate must explain to the person that he is not obliged to confess and that any confession may be used as evidence, and the Magistrate must be satisfied that it was made voluntarily and must note this in a memorandum (section 164(3)). If a Magistrate fails to follow those requirements, section 533(1) allows the court to require the accused to make the statement again and permits admission of the statement unless the error injured the defence. The extracts contain no provision describing safeguards for statements made to the police, so no comparison can be made from the given material.

citations.quote: A Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so it may be used as evidence against him

If any Court, before which a confession or other statement of an accused person recorded or purporting to be recorded under section 164 or section 364 is tendered or has been received in evidence, finds that any of the provisions of either of such sections have not been complied with by the Magistrate recording the statement, it shall take evidence that such person duly make the statement recorded; and, notwithstanding anything contained in the Evidence Act, 1872, section 91, such statement shall be admitted if the error has not injured the accused as to his defence on the merits.

text: After a complaint is filed, the magistrate must first examine the complainant (and any witnesses) and record the substance of that examination in writing. After a person is arrested, the officer who has custody (an Executive Magistrate, District Superintendent of Police or Police Commissioner) must first verify that the arrested person is the one named in the warrant and then "direct his removal in custody to such Court" (section 86). If the offence is bailable and the accused is ready to give bail, the officer "shall take such bail or security" and forward the bond to the issuing court; if the offence is non‑bailable, the Sessions Judge or a first‑class Magistrate may, at his discretion, release the person on interim bail and direct appearance before the court (section 86). 

Once before the Magistrate, the Magistrate (or a specially‑empowered Magistrate) may "record any statement or confession made to him in the course of an investigation" (section 164). The Magistrate then proceeds with the inquiry or trial. If a new Magistrate takes over, he may "act on the evidence so recorded by his predecessor, or partly recorded by his predecessor and partly recorded by himself; or he may re‑summon the witnesses" (section 350). The Court must "record the facts constituting the offence, with the statement (if any) made by the offender, as well as the finding and sentence" (section 481). On the date fixed for trial, the Court "shall proceed to take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution" (section 265G). Finally, if the accused is found capable of making his defence, "the inquiry or trial shall proceed"; otherwise the Magistrate follows the provisions for persons of unsound mind (section 468).

text: The Code of Criminal Procedure, as amended, allows a police‑officer to make an arrest without a warrant in several situations. An arrest can also be made on a requisition from another police‑officer that specifies the person and the offence and shows that the person could be lawfully arrested without a warrant.
